demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is 33, a married paramedic of European background, and when she first comes in she sits very upright, as if even in the therapy room she is still on shift and waiting for the next call. She speaks carefully at first, with the clipped efficiency of someone who is used to making decisions fast, but the story that brought her here is one she cannot organize neatly. It happened on an ordinary workday, which may be part of why it has lodged in her so deeply: nothing about the scene felt dramatic or extraordinary until the moment it did.

She had been dispatched to what was described as a routine medical emergency. She was moving with her partner through a crowded, noisy space, focused on assessing the situation, clearing a path, keeping the patient stable. In the confusion, with people calling out and equipment shifting in her hands, she made a split-second decision that she still replays over and over. A series of small errors, she says, all reasonable in the moment, came together in the worst possible way. A person was seriously injured because of what she did. She is very precise about that wording. She does not say "it happened" or "there was an accident" unless pressed; she says she caused it. The certainty with which she claims responsibility is striking, and so is the way she holds herself rigidly when she says it, as though any softness would be a kind of betrayal.

In the immediate aftermath, she goes into task mode. She remembers the sound of voices, the look on her partner's face, the urgent scramble to stabilize the injured person, the too-bright sense that time has slowed and sped up at once. She completes the call, returns to work, and tells herself there is no room for anything else. She has spent years in emergency medicine and knows how to function under pressure. At home, she tells her husband only the bare outline at first. He asks if she is all right, and she says yes because that is what she has always said after difficult calls. But that night she cannot sleep. Each time she closes her eyes she sees the moment again, not as a memory but as an event still unfolding. She starts to dread the dark because it gives the scene a place to appear.

In the weeks that follow, she becomes preoccupied with what she missed, what she should have noticed, what her hands did not do quickly enough. She runs the call over in her mind in exhaustive detail, trying to locate the exact second when the outcome might have changed. The effort does not bring clarity; it only deepens her conviction that she should have known. She begins avoiding conversations with coworkers about the incident and feels a sudden coldness when her pager goes off, as if the tone of it alone might mean another irreversible mistake. She notices herself watching patients and equipment with unusual intensity, checking and rechecking everything, especially anything that involves moving a body, transferring a patient, or making a rapid judgment. What once felt automatic now feels dangerous.

Her sleep becomes fragmented. She wakes with her heart racing, sometimes with her jaw clenched so tightly that it aches. She has images that intrude without warning: the injured person on the ground, the expression she reads as shock or pain, the moment before everything went wrong. Sometimes the images are so immediate that she has to grip the edge of a table or step into another room until they pass. She is startled by sirens, by the metallic clatter of a stretcher, by certain phrases on the radio. After shifts she comes home drained and irritable, then feels ashamed for snapping at her husband over nothing. She tells herself she is making him carry her burden and that he deserves better than a wife who comes home half somewhere else.

Over time, she begins to pull away from people at work and at home. She attends family gatherings but feels detached, as if she is listening through glass. She loves her husband and knows that he is trying to help, yet there are moments when she cannot bear his concern because it makes the injury feel present again. She no longer describes work with the same openness; she gives short answers, avoids talking about difficult calls, and feels guilty when she is unable to say more. She also notices a growing dread before each shift, a heavy sensation in her stomach that starts the night before and lingers until she has clocked in. Even then, she is tense, scanning for danger, bracing for the next mistake. She does not trust her own judgment the way she once did.

What stands out most is how much effort it takes her to keep functioning. She still works, still shows up, still performs the tasks that once came naturally, but she does so by force of will. The injury she caused has become a private reference point for nearly everything: the way she drives, the way she touches equipment, the way she measures herself against the possibility of failure. She says she used to think of herself as calm under pressure. Now she says she is only good at appearing calm, and even that feels temporary.
